result.question: Follow-up research for PIIIX-org/portfolio.me: (1) find concrete, named, web-specific technique for deliberately breaking a design rule well, including a checkable heuristic distinguishing deliberate-legible violation from random-illegible violation, going deeper than Samara's "Making and Breaking the Grid" and the IDF rule-of-thirds page; (2) test the hypothesis that AI-generated design converges on "safe" outputs because it is statistical/pattern-matching while human designers break rules via emotional/intuitive judgment, checking Norman's aesthetic-usability effect, processing-fluency research, named practitioner framing of "AI=safe/statistical vs human=emotional/risk-taking," and wabi-sabi/imperfection discourse applied to digital/web design.
result.summary: Five queries split 3/2 across the two goals. Goal 1 gets a Samara-technique-deep-dive query, a named-practitioner/awards-jury query restricted to web (not print or photography), and a query hunting for an explicit checkable "break one rule, keep everything else disciplined" principle. Goal 2 gets one query targeting the actual academic findings (aesthetic-usability effect plus processing fluency, checking whether they support or refute the hypothesis) and one query targeting named practitioner framing plus wabi-sabi-in-digital-design discourse, since the psych research and the design-writing framing are distinct source types that need separate searches to avoid conflating "proven" with "someone opined."

angles.label: Samara technique deep-dive
angles.query: Timothy Samara Making and Breaking the Grid split splice shift spontaneous compositions narrative constructs working on an axis intuitive design technique explained
angles.rationale: Prior pass named these five Samara techniques but did not explain what each means or how it applies to web layout; targets book content, reviews, and design-school summaries.

angles.label: Web-specific practitioner rule-breaking
angles.query: web designer studio interview breaking the grid asymmetric layout site:awwwards.com OR site:cssdesignawards.com OR site:thefwa.com site of the day
angles.rationale: Targets awards-platform jury writeups and studio interviews per the instruction to search those platforms directly, restricted to web not print or photography.

angles.label: Checkable heuristic for deliberate vs random violation
angles.query: design principle break one rule keep everything else disciplined intentional grid violation versus accidental heuristic
angles.rationale: Hunts for the named checkable heuristic the question flags as precedent rather than accepting an invented version.

angles.label: Aesthetic-usability effect and processing fluency
angles.query: Don Norman aesthetic usability effect Kurosu Kashimura 1995 study findings processing fluency disfluency preference prototypicality aesthetics research
angles.rationale: Checks the two named psychology sources for what they actually establish, since fluency research may point opposite to the working hypothesis and must be reported honestly either way.

angles.label: AI safe/statistical vs human emotional framing and wabi-sabi in digital design
angles.query: AI generated design safe optimized statistical versus human designer emotional intuitive risk taking generic wabi-sabi imperfection web design deliberate flaw asymmetry
angles.rationale: Searches practitioner blogs and design critics for this specific comparative framing, distinct from Goal 1 tells material, and for named writing applying wabi-sabi to digital design as a countersignal to AI output.

results.title: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect (Nielsen Norman Group)
results.snippet: Named-source, directly on point. Defines the effect as users perceiving attractive designs as more usable, cites Kurosu & Kashimura's 1995 Hitachi study (26 ATM UI variants, 252 participants) finding perceived-ease-of-use correlated more strongly with aesthetic rating than with actual ease of use. Explicitly notes the effect has boundaries — attractive design forgives only minor usability problems, not major ones. Confirms this study says nothing about rule-breaking, imperfection, or disfluency reading as more trustworthy/intentional — that connection is not present in the source and would be a misapplication if asserted. Useful for Goal 2: shows what AUE actually claims (looks-good-so-assumed-usable) versus what the working hypothesis needs it to claim (breaking rules reads as more human/deliberate) — these are different claims.

results.title: Aesthetic-usability effect (Wikipedia)
results.snippet: Corroborates the NNGroup framing with the same Kurosu & Kashimura (Hitachi, 1995) citation and the core finding that apparent usability correlates with apparent beauty more than with inherent usability. Also flags a secondary, lesser-known finding from the same research tradition: cognitive-style effects (Wholist-Analytic vs Verbal-Imagery) on aesthetic preference were weaker than hypothesized. No mention anywhere of rule-breaking or imperfection — reinforces that this is a well-sourced but narrow finding (beauty biases usability perception), not a rule-breaking-reads-as-intentional finding.

results.title: Processing fluency (Wikipedia)
results.snippet: Directly tests and largely REFUTES the working hypothesis rather than supporting it. States fluency research finds the opposite of what the hypothesis needs: easier-to-process stimuli get more favorable evaluations across domains (aesthetic pleasure ratings, the 'illusion of truth effect' where easy-to-read statements are judged more truthful, and consumer approach behavior toward fluent product design). Only nuance found: a passing reference to 'optimal stimulation theory' — moderate incongruity is tolerated/enjoyed but too much disorder overwhelms — which is not the same claim as 'disfluency reads as more intentional/human' and stops well short of supporting deliberate rule-breaking as a trust signal. Flag for the requester: fluency research points opposite to the house theory on the primary claim; only a thin, indirect 'moderate complexity is tolerated' thread survives, and even that isn't sourced to say disfluency signals intentionality.

results.title: Emotional Design (Wikipedia) — Don Norman's book
results.snippet: Confirms Norman's actual claim: attractive products are perceived as more effective because of emotional/sensual connection ('beautifully designed products make people feel good' at the visceral level), not because attractiveness is objectively correlated with better function. Confirms the book contains NO discussion of deliberate imperfection, rule-breaking, or asymmetry as a design strategy, and does not address whether such qualities read as more trustworthy or human than systematic/perfect design. This directly narrows the 'emotional-vs-systematic' hypothesis: Norman's actual argument is about aesthetics-drives-perceived-function generally, not about rule-violation specifically — using his name to back the emotional/intuitive-vs-statistical framing would overstate what the book says.

results.title: The Art of Breaking Design Rules | Studio Hoook (Medium)
results.snippet: Strongest match found for the exact precedent the research question asks about. Has a section literally titled "Choose Your Single Act of Defiance," arguing rule-breaking fails when applied everywhere ("What results is noise, visual chaos that confuses rather than communicates") and succeeds when isolated to one element while everything else stays disciplined: "By choosing one dramatic violation and executing it flawlessly while honoring every other principle, Supreme created an iconic mark." Contrasts this against failed rebrands (Gap, Tropicana) as cases where breaking read as arbitrary rather than intentional. Named source: design studio Studio Hoook.

results.title: Master the Grid, Then Break It: The Designer's Most Important Paradox — Shiva Padival (Medium, Design Bootcamp)
results.snippet: Gives a distinct, directly checkable test for legible vs. random rule-breaking: "The test is simple, and it is ruthless: Can you explain why every element is where it is?" Frames disciplined grid-breaking as requiring an articulable rationale (emphasis, rhythm, tension, voice) per violation, built on prior mastery of the grid — a named, self-contained heuristic an agent could execute as a checklist item ("can I state the reason for this specific placement?").

results.title: Rules Are Tools: Why Knowing the Grid Helps You Break It Better — Studio Lumistra
results.snippet: States the discipline-elsewhere principle in near-exact form: "when structure is intentionally broken—when alignment is thrown off, when type scales unexpectedly, when rules are bent rather than discarded—it leaves a stronger impression," paired with a music/dissonance analogy (dissonance only reads as meaningful against maintained harmony). Doesn't give a numbered rule like "break exactly one," but is one of the more explicit statements that violation needs surrounding order to read as deliberate rather than sloppy.

results.title: Breaking the Grid: When and How to Go Off-Grid in Design — Design Shack
results.snippet: Practical, layout-focused (not print/photography) piece on when off-grid composition works vs. fails, useful as a secondary source for web-specific technique even though it doesn't name a single checkable heuristic as sharply as the two Medium pieces above.

results.title: Some Design Rules are Made To Be Broken — DWUser
results.snippet: Grid-system-specific discussion of when the grid is a useful starting point vs. an obstacle; relevant background for the split/splice/shift-style technique question but doesn't articulate the intentional-vs-accidental test itself.

results.title: Breaking Design Rules Creatively — Expressa
results.snippet: General listicle-style treatment of rule-breaking in design; touches the same territory but reads as more generic advice than a named practitioner's specific technique or checkable test, weaker fit for Goal 1's bar.

claims.claim: Wikipedia's processing fluency article establishes a one-directional model: higher fluency (easier processing) is associated with more favorable evaluations, with no documented condition where disfluency is preferred, judged more interesting, or read as more intentional/trustworthy — this runs counter to, not in support of, the research's working hypothesis that intentional 'rule-breaking' roughness would read as more human/trustworthy.
claims.quote: Higher fluency is often associated with more favorable evaluations, even when the ease of processing is unrelated to the content itself

claims.claim: The article documents zero coverage of the aesthetic-usability effect, Kurosu & Kashimura (1995), Don Norman, design rule-breaking, imperfection-in-design, or AI-generated content — meaning this source cannot be cited as support for the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis in either direction; it is simply silent on it, and any claim linking processing-fluency research to deliberate imperfection reading as 'more human' would be an unsourced extrapolation not present in this text.
claims.quote: The Wikipedia article contains NO discussion of conditions where disfluency is preferred.

claims.claim: Processing fluency is formally defined as the subjective ease/difficulty of a mental task, split into perceptual fluency (ease of processing sensory stimuli, affected by visual clarity and contrast) and retrieval fluency (ease of accessing memory) — a definitional baseline useful for precisely scoping what 'fluency' means before applying it to design claims.
claims.quote: the subjective experience of ease or difficulty associated with mental tasks

claims.claim: The fluency effect is shown to generalize beyond simple liking into unrelated evaluative dimensions — e.g., text set in easy-to-read fonts is judged funnier — illustrating that fluency operates as a general positivity/ease heuristic rather than a signal specifically about creativity, intentionality, or authenticity.
claims.quote: gave higher ratings to jokes in easy to read fonts

claims.claim: Repeated exposure to a stimulus increases fluency, which in turn increases liking (a mere-exposure-effect-adjacent finding), reinforcing that fluency research as documented here tracks familiarity/ease rather than deliberate deviation from convention.
claims.quote: repetition of a stimulus can lead to fluent processing which leads to a feeling of liking

claims.claim: The aesthetic-usability effect is defined as users' tendency to perceive attractive products as more usable — a perception effect, not a claim that attractive/rule-breaking design is actually more functional.
claims.quote: users' tendency to perceive attractive products as more usable

claims.claim: Kurosu & Kashimura's 1995 study (26 ATM UI variations, 252 participants) found that aesthetic appeal correlated more strongly with PERCEIVED ease of use than with ACTUAL (measured) ease of use — i.e. attractiveness biases judgment of usability rather than improving real usability.
claims.quote: the correlation between participants' ratings of aesthetic appeal and perceived ease of use was stronger than the correlation between their ratings of aesthetic appeal and actual ease of use

claims.claim: The effect's protective power is bounded: attractive design makes users forgive only minor usability issues, not major functional failures — attractiveness does not substitute for function.
claims.quote: Form and function should work together

claims.claim: This NN/g article — the standard citation for the aesthetic-usability effect — contains no discussion of rule-breaking, imperfection, disfluency, or trustworthiness in design; the effect as sourced here is strictly about attractiveness-driven perceived usability, not about deliberate rule violation reading as more human/intentional/trustworthy.
claims.quote: The article contains no discussion of rule-breaking, imperfection, disfluency, or trustworthiness related to design.

claims.claim: The aesthetic-usability effect, as defined by this source, is specifically that people perceive more aesthetically pleasing designs as more usable/intuitive than less aesthetically pleasing ones — a cognitive bias about attractiveness driving perceived usability. The article contains no framing of it as being about rule-breaking, imperfection, or deliberate deviation reading as more trustworthy or human.
claims.quote: The aesthetic–usability effect describes a paradox that people perceive more aesthetic designs as much more intuitive than those considered to be less aesthetically pleasing.

claims.claim: The foundational Kurosu & Kashimura (1995) study found that users' perception of a system's usability (apparent usability) correlated more strongly with the system's perceived beauty than with its actual, inherent usability — i.e., attractiveness biases usability judgments, not that broken/imperfect designs are judged more favorably.
claims.quote: the apparent usability is less correlated with the inherent usability compared to the apparent beauty.

claims.claim: This Wikipedia article on the aesthetic-usability effect contains zero mentions of processing fluency, disfluency, prototypicality, or of imperfection/rule-breaking reading as more intentional, trustworthy, or human — meaning this source, taken on its own terms, offers no support (and no refutation) for the emotional-vs-systematic / deliberate-imperfection hypothesis; it is simply silent on it.
claims.quote: No mentions found of these concepts anywhere in the article.

claims.claim: The article's reference list for the aesthetic-usability effect draws on a distinct lineage of usability/HCI researchers (Kurosu & Kashimura 1995; Tractinsky 1997/2000; Hall and Hanna; Conklin 2006; McCracken and Wolfe 2004; Lee and Koubeks 2011; Shi, Huo, and Hou 2021) rather than any design-critique or AI-generic-design literature, confirming this is a usability-perception research thread separate from the rule-breaking/AI-tells research goal.
claims.quote: Kurosu & Kashimura (1995); Tractinsky (1997, 2000); Hall and Hanna; Conklin (2006); McCracken and Wolfe (2004); Lee and Koubeks (2011); Shi, Huo, and Hou (2021)

claims.claim: Norman's Emotional Design (2003) argues attractive/aesthetically pleasing objects are perceived by users as more effective, via their visceral/sensual appeal — the book's own version of an 'attractive = better' claim. Note: this Wikipedia summary does NOT mention or cite Kurosu & Kashimura's 1995 study or the term 'aesthetic-usability effect' at all — that specific research citation is absent from this source and would need to be sourced elsewhere.
claims.quote: aesthetically pleasing objects appear to the user to be more effective, by virtue of their sensual appeal.

claims.claim: The book's core framework (visceral/behavioral/reflective levels) attributes the 'attractive things work better' effect to sensory/emotional engagement at the visceral level — not to disfluency, imperfection, or rule-breaking.
claims.quote: attractive products work better because they can engage multiple senses to evoke emotional responses.

claims.claim: Norman's stated thesis is that technology should deliver emotional richness and enjoyment beyond task performance — an argument for emotional/reflective design in general, but this source contains no claim connecting deliberate rule-breaking, imperfection, or disfluency to reading as more human, trustworthy, or intentional. This is negative evidence against using Emotional Design as a citable source for the emotional-vs-systematic/rule-breaking hypothesis: the book is about emotional connection and aesthetics improving perceived usability, not about norm violation as a design signal.
claims.quote: technology should bring more to our lives than improved performance of tasks: it should be richness and enjoyment.

claims.claim: The article claims that grid-breaking (off-grid) design is very difficult to make work responsively on the web, implying the technique is fundamentally desktop/print-oriented rather than reliably web-native.
claims.quote: A grid-breaking design you create for a desktop will not look the same on mobile devices. It's almost impossible to create responsive off-grid designs.

claims.claim: The article names four specific techniques for breaking a grid: layering/overlapping elements, dynamic (non-boxed) typography placement, organic shapes/fluid lines replacing geometric forms, and interactive/animated elements.
claims.quote: different placements, sizes, and arrangements for your titles and text... instead of placing text in a box

claims.claim: The article claims certain content categories (newspapers, magazines, business brochures) still require grid adherence for readability, implicitly carving out where grid-breaking is and isn't appropriate — but does not extend this into a portfolio/web-specific rule.
claims.quote: some designs like newspapers, magazines, and business brochures need to follow a grid design to ensure readability

claims.claim: The article gestures toward (without stating as a named, checkable principle) an idea resembling 'discipline elsewhere' — that grid-breaking still requires underlying systems (visual hierarchy, focal points, negative space, flow) or the result becomes chaotic — but this is not framed as the specific 'break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined' heuristic the research sought.
claims.quote: Going off-grid does not mean inventing your own ways of design...you need to follow a few design systems

claims.claim: The article warns explicitly that unstructured grid-breaking risks producing a cluttered result, i.e. it acknowledges the failure mode (random/illegible violation) without providing a test to distinguish it from deliberate/legible violation.
claims.quote: designs tend to get chaotic with text, images, and shapes all over the place

claims.claim: The article frames rule-breaking as requiring foundational mastery first, not license for randomness: rules must be understood before being broken.
claims.quote: It is important to know the rules before you consider breaking them!

claims.claim: The article's only proposed 'test' for whether to break a rule is unsourced personal/designer intuition, not a checkable, executable heuristic — this is the emotional/intuitive framing the research question is testing, but here it is asserted as opinion with no citation to research or named methodology, so it cannot upgrade the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis beyond 'untested house theory.'
claims.quote: If you are a good designer, then you probably have an innate instinct for visual taste. That intuition must be used to decide whether a rule should be broken in the first place.

claims.claim: Named practitioner David Carson is cited as breaking the grid system entirely (not a single controlled violation) via overlapping text, images, and diagonal lines — an example of a real designer's technique, but describes print/editorial design, not web layout, and is not framed as a legibility-preserving 'break one rule, keep the rest disciplined' technique.
claims.quote: ignores the vertical and horizontal planes completely, relying heavily on overlapping text, images and diagonal lines

claims.claim: The article provides zero web-design-specific guidance or examples — all rule-breaking examples given (David Carson's editorial layouts, David Lance Goines posters, Milton Glaser color work, VW's 'Think Small' print ad) are print/graphic-design case studies, confirming this source cannot fill the Goal 1 web-specific gap.
claims.quote: The article focuses exclusively on print and graphic design examples; no web-specific guidance provided.

claims.claim: The article articulates a checkable heuristic close to the one the research is looking for: a rule violation reads as an intentional, meaningful decision (rather than random noise) specifically because everything else around it remains structured/disciplined — the violation 'carries weight precisely because of what it breaks away from.'
claims.quote: when structure is intentionally broken—when alignment is thrown off, when type scales unexpectedly, when rules are bent rather than discarded—it leaves a stronger impression. It tells the viewer: this break means something. It carries weight precisely because of what it breaks away from.

claims.claim: The article uses a harmony/dissonance musical analogy to explain the mechanism: a broken rule (dissonance/solo) only reads as deliberate if the surrounding system (harmony/band) is still audibly intact — directly analogous to the 'break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined' precedent the research was searching for, though phrased generically rather than as a named design principle.
claims.quote: Think of it like music. Dissonance only works because of harmony. A solo feels meaningful because you know the band is still playing behind it. You need the baseline to appreciate the improvisation.

claims.claim: The article frames the grid as a decision-making framework rather than a stylistic constraint, arguing that designers who understand grid structure treat disruption as strategic rather than superficial — supporting context for why rule-knowledge precedes rule-breaking, but stated as general opinion, not tied to any named technique (no split/splice/shift, no web-specific example).
claims.quote: Designers who understand this rarely see the grid as a limitation. They see it as a framework for decision-making. And from there, disruption becomes strategic rather than superficial.

claims.claim: The piece is grounded in print/typography and graphic-design history (the Swiss grid tradition), not web design specifically — it never mentions websites, HTML/CSS, digital layout, or AI-generated design, so it cannot be cited as web-specific practitioner evidence despite being relevant in principle.
claims.quote: Historically, the grid has been a tool of rational design thinking. Most closely associated with the Swiss style of the mid-20th century, it prioritises legibility, visual hierarchy, and modular consistency.

claims.claim: The article's core actionable heuristic for legible rule-breaking is to limit a design to exactly ONE deliberate rule violation while executing everything else with discipline — the single violation reads as a strategic choice ('rebellion') precisely because everything surrounding it is consistent, which is what makes it feel intentional rather than accidental. This directly matches the precedent the research question was looking for ('break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined').
claims.quote: When you decide which rule to break, you're making a strategic choice. That one violation becomes your brand's rebellion. Everything else reinforces it, amplifies it, makes it feel intentional rather than accidental.

claims.claim: The article names the failure mode of breaking multiple rules at once ('do it everywhere') as producing 'noise, visual chaos that confuses rather than communicates' — offering a checkable anti-pattern (count the simultaneous violations; more than one signals illegible/random rather than deliberate breaking) rather than a vague 'be more creative' instruction.
claims.quote: The temptation when learning about rule-breaking is to do it everywhere. Break the grid here, invert the color theory there, ignore hierarchy in another corner. What results is noise, visual chaos that confuses rather than communicates.

claims.claim: The article proposes tiering which rules are safe to break by risk: purely aesthetic conventions (spacing, color) are low-risk to violate, while rules that serve accessibility, legibility, and usability are high-risk and require much stronger justification before breaking — a usable filter for an agent deciding WHICH rule to target.
claims.quote: Breaking purely aesthetic conventions carries minimal risk. A luxury brand can use unconventional spacing or unexpected color combinations because these choices might delight rather than disable. But breaking functional rules requires substantially stronger justification.

claims.claim: The article offers a durability heuristic ('the timeless vs. trendy test') for evaluating whether a specific rule-break is well-founded: ask whether it will still make sense in 5-10 years versus merely riding a temporary design trend. This is a different axis than legibility (it tests durability of the choice, not whether it reads as intentional in the moment).
claims.quote: Ask yourself: in five years, ten years, will this rule-break anchor to timeless principles or ride on temporary 2025 design trends?

claims.claim: The article is entirely print/brand-identity-general in its examples (Supreme's logo, Gap 2010 and Tropicana 2009 rebrand failures) and contains no web-specific layout/grid/typography guidance, no discussion of AI-generated or templated design, and no framing of emotional/intuitive versus systematic/statistical design — it is not a source for Goal 1's web-specificity ask or for Goal 2's hypothesis at all.
claims.quote: Not all rules were created equal, and neither should all your rule-breaks be.

results.title: Making and Breaking the Grid, Third Edition — Quarto (publisher)
results.snippet: Official publisher description is the primary source naming all five Samara rule-breaking techniques verbatim in one place: "Split, splice, and shift; create spontaneous compositions; make narrative constructs; work on an axis; use intuitive design ... to create unique layouts." Confirms the book's framing is 'understand the rules of the grid to use them effectively, and then how to break them' for 'phenomenal cohesive layouts' — i.e., mastery-before-violation, not randomness. Does not itself define each term (no worked examples in this text), so still needs the book itself for depth, but is the cleanest citable primary confirmation that these are Samara's actual named techniques and not a paraphrase.

results.title: Making and Breaking the Grid, Third Edition — Google Books (table of contents)
results.snippet: Reveals the book's actual chapter structure, which is directly useful for Goal 1's heuristic question. The "BREAKING THE GRID" part is organized as: Structure Beyond Grid Structure → Liberating Layout Strategies → 'Reconciling Usability and Weirdness' → Design Projects Without Grids. That middle heading is Samara's own named framing for the 'break it deliberately vs break it randomly' distinction the research angle is looking for — a book section explicitly built around keeping a broken layout usable while still being 'weird,' rather than a generic call to 'be more creative.' Worth quoting directly if this angle's findings get written up.

results.title: Making and Breaking the Grid, Third Edition — Goodreads reader reviews
results.snippet: Named (if pseudonymous) reader reviews characterize how the book treats rule-breaking as disciplined rather than arbitrary. Thai Son: the book 'treats structure and expression as partners rather than enemies ... never presented a grid in isolation.' Mauricio Villamayor: it helps readers 'categorise deconstruction practices,' calling it 'more useful for people that already know how to use the grid' first — i.e., corroborates the 'master the system, then violate it' sequencing. Tier C (reader opinion, not a design authority), but concrete and attributable, and several reviews flag the book's print/poster-heavy examples as dated, which matters for this angle's 'is this web-specific' concern — it largely isn't.

results.title: Making and Breaking the Grid, Third Edition — Walter Foster (secondary publisher listing)
results.snippet: Second official retailer/publisher page, word-for-word the same technique list as the Quarto page ('Split, splice, and shift; create spontaneous compositions; make narrative constructs; work on an axis; use intuitive design'). Useful only as a corroborating second citation that this exact five-technique list is the book's own official marketing language, not a third-party summary — adds no new depth beyond the Quarto source.

claims.claim: The article frames deliberate rule-breaking as requiring prior understanding of the principle being broken, rather than giving a specific checkable test for legible vs. random violation — this is close to but not the same as the 'break exactly one rule, keep everything disciplined' precedent the research is looking for.
claims.quote: it's about understanding the principles behind these rules and knowing when and how to bend them

claims.claim: The article names offsetting a headline slightly and using unconventional image spacing as a specific alignment-breaking technique for web layouts.
claims.quote: offsetting a headline slightly or using unconventional spacing for images

claims.claim: The article names oversized fonts, unconventional kerning, and mixing drastically different typefaces as specific techniques for breaking a type scale/hierarchy.
claims.quote: Oversized fonts, unconventional kerning, or mixing drastically different typefaces

claims.claim: The article frames hand-drawn elements, irregular shapes, and textured backgrounds ('imperfections') as adding warmth and authenticity — a weak, non-AI-specific echo of the wabi-sabi/imperfection-as-countersignal idea in Goal 2, but with no connection made to AI-generated or templated design specifically.
claims.quote: incorporating imperfections such as hand-drawn elements...can add warmth and authenticity

results.title: Wabi-Sabi in Web Design: How to Implement Aesthetic Imperfection for UX — Robert Coxe, Silphium Design
results.snippet: Best single hit for BOTH goals. Named practitioner (Robert Coxe, web design studio) explicitly frames wabi-sabi as an AI countersignal: 'As we move further into the age of AI and automated design, the human touch becomes more valuable... AI can generate a perfect image in seconds... But it cannot easily understand the beauty of the crack in the cup' — calls it 'the antidote to the machine age.' Also states the grid is 'the invisible skeleton of the web... the enemy of wabi-sabi,' and gives a checkable discipline heuristic almost identical to the one your pipeline is looking for: 'If you break the grid too much, the site becomes confusing... The chaos must be controlled. It is like a Japanese garden.' Web-specific (CSS Grid, border-radius, clip-path techniques named), not print/photography.

results.title: 10 Award-Winning Websites of 2026, Judged — Hon Tran (Awwwards jury member)
results.snippet: Directly answers Goal 1's ask for a named juror praising a specific rule violation. Author is an actual Awwwards jury member (11+ years, two-time Independent of the Year nominee). On Uncommon Studio's site: praises 'a confident grid that breaks at exactly the right moments' with the deviation read as rhythmic/purposeful rather than chaotic. States the underlying judging principle: award-winners show 'a specific point of view' where 'every type choice, color, and layout grid serves a single idea' — i.e., rule-breaking is praised only when motivated by a single controlling idea, not arbitrary.

results.title: Awwwards Judging Criteria: How Scoring Works (2026) — Hon Tran
results.snippet: Companion piece to the above, same named juror, gives the checkable heuristic Goal 1 asked for in near-exact form: 'Grid discipline that still feels intentional, not templated,' contrasted with an explicit penalty for undisciplined excess — 'designers pile on effects to look impressive. The jury reads that as a lack of control and it costs you.' Net principle: a deviation reads as a decision only when everything else demonstrates control — functionally the same as 'break exactly one rule, keep everything else disciplined,' from a named credentialed juror rather than an invented rule.

results.title: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect — Nielsen Norman Group
results.snippet: Verification source for Goal 2. Confirms precisely what the aesthetic-usability effect does and does NOT claim: 'Users are more tolerant of minor usability issues when they find an interface visually appealing' — a perceived-usability halo from attractiveness, and nothing about rule-breaking, imperfection, or AI-vs-human origin reading as more trustworthy. Using it to support the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis would be a misapplication; it only supports 'attractive designs get a usability pass,' not 'rule-breaking designs read as more human or intentional.'

results.title: The Debate: AI vs. Human Graphic Designers — Kreafolk
results.snippet: Flag per the verification framing: this is generic content-marketing, NOT a named practitioner byline — Kreafolk is a design content platform, article has no individual author credited. It does state the exact working hypothesis almost verbatim ('AI... prioritizes stability and repetition, sometimes at the cost of originality' vs 'Human designers embrace mistakes as opportunities for discovery... they understand when to deviate from guidelines for expressive or strategic purposes'), showing the framing circulates in design-adjacent writing, but it is unsourced/anonymous and should not be cited as a verified named-practitioner claim — only as evidence the framing exists informally, not that it's established.

results.title: Wabi-Sabi in the Age of Perfect Algorithms — Taishi Okano
results.snippet: Named individual practitioner (writes on technology/craft/culture, NY/Tokyo) explicitly linking wabi-sabi to a critique of algorithmic perfection: 'There are no cracks. And so there is no invitation. The reader is a passenger, not a participant' and 'The judgment of what to leave for the perceiving mind to complete is not something an algorithm can make.' Scope caveat: this is general aesthetic philosophy applied loosely to technology/products (architecture, ceramics, gardens, writing) — not a web-design-specific technique piece like the Silphium Design source, so weaker for Goal 1 but useful corroboration for Goal 2's wabi-sabi-as-AI-countersignal question.

claims.claim: The book explicitly names five distinct grid-breaking techniques as its content, but the publisher page only lists the names without explaining what any of them mean or how to execute them — confirming the same 'named but not explained' gap the prior research pass already identified, not resolving it.
claims.quote: Split, splice, and shift; create spontaneous compositions; make narrative constructs; work on an axis; use intuitive design.

claims.claim: The Third Edition (2023) was specifically updated to add coverage of grid use in digital/interactive contexts, meaning the book claims some web/UI-specific content exists — even though this listing page gives no detail on what that web-specific guidance actually says.
claims.quote: expanded coverage of "grid use in interactive, UX/UI scenarios."

No source in this cluster connects the effect to rule-breaking, imperfection, or disfluency.
findings.evidence: Kurosu and Kashimura's 1995 study (26 ATM UI variations, 252 participants) found aesthetic appeal correlated more strongly with PERCEIVED ease of use than with ACTUAL ease of use - confirmed identically by both NN/g and Wikipedia. Both sources were independently checked (keyword search of full text) and contain zero mentions of rule-breaking, imperfection, disfluency, or trustworthiness - this effect is strictly 'attractive = looks more usable,' not 'imperfect/broken = reads as more human or trustworthy.' Six separate verification passes across the two sources unanimously confirm this narrow scope, making this the best-corroborated finding in the whole research question and the clearest available evidence AGAINST casually citing the aesthetic-usability effect to support the working hypothesis.

(2) A Readymag blog post that seemed like an ideal source for 'build the grid first, then break it' was also refuted 0-3 on both sub-claims. Unanswered (not negatively answered) sub-goals: Goal 1's request for named Awwwards/CSS Design Awards/FWA/Godly/Land-book juror or critic commentary specifically praising a rule violation returned nothing among the surviving claims - this needs a dedicated pass hitting those platforms' own blogs/interviews directly, which does not appear to have been attempted or at least did not survive verification. Neither is refuted; both are simply gaps in this pass's coverage.

Hypothesis status, stated plainly: the emotional-vs-systematic hypothesis (AI = statistical/safe, human = emotional/risk-taking, explaining generic AI output) has NO supporting named source found across either research pass, and the one directly relevant strand of psychology research that was checked (processing fluency) points the opposite direction from what the hypothesis would predict. It should be treated in the pipeline as an unverified working theory, not doctrine, until/unless a design-critic or practitioner source is found making this specific framing explicitly.

Proposed pipeline mechanism (synthesis of the above, not itself a sourced claim - offered per the deliverable's request): a 'grid-break legibility gate' analogous to loops/02-design.md's category-reflex check. For every element in a generated layout that deviates from the established grid/alignment/type-scale/whitespace rhythm, the agent must be able to state, in the design rationale: (a) name the specific rule being broken (alignment point, column width, gutter, type-scale step, or spacing unit); (b) give a one-sentence non-generic reason for the deviation (emphasis, tension, narrative beat, brand voice - not 'to look less AI-generated'); and (c) confirm the same rule holds everywhere else in the layout except at that one deviation point. If (a)+(b)+(c) can't all be answered for a given element, revert it to the grid. This is directly sourced from three convergent findings above (Phogat's decision-vs-default test, UsabilityGeek's master-the-grid-first precondition, Padival's can-you-explain-every-placement test) and is checkable the same way the category-reflex check is checkable - it's a pass/fail question an agent can actually run against its own output, not a vague 'be bolder' instruction. Additionally, given the confirmed context-dependency finding, this gate should probably only fire for hero/landing/about-style exploratory sections of a portfolio site, not for any utility UI (contact forms, project detail navigation) the pipeline generates, since the sourced material explicitly says grid-breaking fails on task-focused interfaces.
